newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kleinwort head resigns in Dresdner strategy battle.
newsitem.headline: Kleinwort head resigns in Dresdner strategy battle.

text.p: Germany's second largest bank, Dresdner Bank AG, said on Friday the head of its London-based investment banking unit Kleinwort Benson had resigned from his post due to insurmountable differences over future strategy.

Dresdner said in a statement that Simon Robertson's departure, which was by mutual consent, was due to "different views on the strategic and organisational direction of the investment banking activities of the Dresdner Bank group."

Chief executive Juergen Sarrazin defended Robertson's performance, but said the bank now had to push ahead with integrating its activities in London and Frankfurt. He stressed management would not be concentrated in either centre.

"All of us are agreed that, to recognise the full potential of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, we must now fully integrate our resources in London and Frankfurt, so that they and all our other offices operate as one entity," Sarrazin said.
"Sadly, we have differed with Simon about the way this is best achieved," he added.
"We do not want to concentrate our management in London, in Frankfurt or in any one location. To act that way would be too narrow," Sarrazin said.
A Dresdner spokeswoman in London said Robertson had argued in favour of grouping investment activities in the City.
"The disagreement was basically about how we should go forward in managing the integration process... The two views were irreconcilable," she said.
"Simon Robertson felt that the whole investment banking operation should be managed out of London. We felt we were trying to build up a global banking business," she added.
Banking sources confirmed that Robertson had wanted to seize control of key areas of the bank's overall investment banking activities which were currently run from Germany.

"Kleinwort Benson wanted to become the global leader in areas such as structured finance, project financing and leasing," one source close to the bank said. "Dresdner had not wanted to give these up."
A Dresdner Bank source, who declined to be named, confirmed the essence of these remarks.

"Dresdner Bank took global financing and global markets into the partnership as its contributed strengths," the source said. "We are more effective with a joint team in London and Frankfurt, keeping two centres."

Dresdner acquired the British bank two years ago, in a one billion sterling takeover aimed at strengthening its global investment banking business in the face of growing competition from its larger domestic competitor Deutsche Bank AG.
Analysts then believed that Dresdner had felt compelled to act after Deutsche concentrated its investment banking activities at its British unit Morgan Grenfell.

Dresdner, which said from the start that Kleinwort would remain autonomous within the Dresdner group and be managed as a separate unit in line with the group's business policy, further cemented its split-site strategy with today's announcement.
Eton-educated Robertson, 55, joined Kleinwort in 1963 and only became chairman in March 1996, succeeding Lord Rockley.
At the time he was described as an unanimous choice and "an investment banker's investment banker."
The shake-up of the Kleinwort management board that went along with Robertson's appointment left it dominated by Kleinwort executives, with only one from Dresdner.

Seizing the opportunity offered by Robertson's departure to alter Kleinwort's top management structures, Dresdner said Lord Walker would replace Robertson, but in the position of Non-Executive Chairman.
Excutive control passes to Hansgeorg Hoffmann, who will chair the newly created Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Executive Committee. David Clementi remains Chief Executive at the bank.
The Dresdner source confirmed that the excutive committee would now be the main base of executive power.
Both Sarrazin and the Dresdner source stressed that the disagreement with Robertson was not related to his performance.
"We are sorry to see him leave and wish him well," Sarrazin said.
